title: Money Leaks Beyond Subscriptions: Worked Examples (2026)
metaDescription: Money leaks go beyond subscriptions: delivery fees, repeat impulse buys and yearly renewals. See illustrative rupee examples worked out per month and per year.
h1: What counts as a money leak, and how much can small spends cost?
summary: A money leak is a small, recurring or habitual expense that drains your money without giving you much value in return. Subscriptions are one kind, but delivery fees, repeat impulse buys and once-a-year renewals leak money too. Multiply a monthly leak by 12 to get its yearly cost, then add the leaks together to see the total.

sections.heading: What a money leak is
paragraphs: Money leak is an informal personal finance term, not a formal one. Outlook Money describes how many people lose money through unnoticed daily expenses, such as unused subscriptions, impulse buys and lifestyle upgrades, rather than through big mistakes. Whether something is a leak depends on how much value you get back, so the test is personal.
list: Subscriptions and memberships you no longer use.
Delivery and convenience fees that add up over a month.
Once-a-year bills, such as insurance premiums or property tax, that arrive without a plan for them.

sections.heading: Worked examples (illustrative)
paragraphs: Every figure in this section is hypothetical. The numbers are chosen to make the arithmetic clear and are not averages, survey results or forecasts. Replace them with your own statement totals.
Each example multiplies a monthly amount by 12 for a yearly figure. The combined example adds the monthly amounts first.
list: A ₹299 streaming plan you stopped using: ₹299 × 12 = ₹3,588 a year.
A ₹199 app subscription you forgot about: ₹199 × 12 = ₹2,388 a year.
₹40 delivery fees on 12 orders a month: ₹40 × 12 = ₹480 a month, or ₹5,760 a year.
All three together: ₹299 + ₹199 + ₹480 = ₹978 a month, or ₹978 × 12 = ₹11,736 a year. Over five years, with no price increases, that is ₹58,680.

sections.heading: Why leaks are easy to miss
paragraphs: Small recurring charges rarely feel like spending because there is no moment of payment. Axio argues that people track small everyday purchases closely, such as a coffee or a food delivery, while the recurring charges and yearly bills that cost more slip through unnoticed.

Tracking every small item is not necessarily the answer. Axio notes that logging every coffee and ride adds mental effort, and people who find it a chore often give up. Focusing on recurring payments and bulk yearly bills first is usually more useful.

sections.heading: Where to look first
paragraphs: Start with payments that repeat rather than with every purchase. Your bank or card statements for the last few months, and the AutoPay or Mandates section of each UPI app you use, will show most recurring leaks. The full quarterly checklist, with timings, is in the subscription audit guide on this site.

sections.heading: How tracking renewals in Essara helps
paragraphs: Essara is a manual tracker. You add each subscription, bill or yearly renewal yourself, and it turns them into monthly and yearly totals with a renewal timeline. It does not connect to your bank, UPI app or SMS. For a quick estimate of what your leaks cost each month, Essara's free monthly money leak calculator is a good starting point.

faqs.a: They can be. An annual insurance premium or property tax is not a leak if you need the cover. A yearly plan you no longer use is. The leak is the value you do not get back, not the size of the bill.

faqs.q: Are money leaks the same as subscription creep?
faqs.a: Subscription creep is one kind of leak: recurring charges that build up unnoticed. Delivery fees and impulse buys are leaks that are not subscriptions. The subscription creep guide covers the recurring kind in more depth.

faqs.q: How much do money leaks cost in a year?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on your own statements, so there is no reliable typical figure. Add up your recurring payments for one month and multiply by 12 for a clear estimate of your situation.

faqs.q: Should I track every expense to find money leaks?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Axio argues that over-tracking small items can cost more attention than it saves. Start with the recurring payments, then review the rest only if you want more detail.
